questions.question: The Sabarmati river originates from which of the following places?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aravalli Hills, Rajasthan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Sabarmati River originates from the **Aravalli Hills** near Udaipur in the Indian state of Rajasthan.
 
• It flows through the Indian states of **Rajasthan** and **Gujarat** before emptying into the Arabian Sea.
 
• The river has a total length of approximately **371 km**, with 48 km in Rajasthan and 323 km in Gujarat.
 
• The Sabarmati is one of the major west-flowing rivers in India, and it plays an important role in the irrigation and water supply of the region.
 
• It is fed by two major tributaries: the **Sedhi River** and the **Wakal River**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Aravalli Hills:**

 
 
• The Aravalli Hills are one of the oldest fold mountain ranges in the world, extending across Rajasthan, Haryana, and Gujarat.
 
• They are known for their unique geology and are rich in mineral resources.
 
• The hills play a critical role in influencing the climatic conditions of the surrounding areas.
 
 
 
• **Sabarmati River Basin:**
 
 
• The Sabarmati basin covers an area of approximately **21,674 sq. km**, making it an important drainage system in western India.
 
• The basin supports agriculture and industries, especially in Gujarat, where cities like Ahmedabad are located along the river.
 
 
 
• **Importance of the Sabarmati:**
 
 
• The Sabarmati Riverfront Development Project in Ahmedabad has turned the river into a model of urban riverfront development.
 
• The river is also culturally significant as it is associated with Mahatma Gandhi’s Sabarmati Ashram.
 
 
 
• **West-Flowing Rivers in India:**
 
 
• Unlike most rivers in India that flow eastward, Sabarmati is among the few west-flowing rivers that drain into the Arabian Sea.
 
• Other major west-flowing rivers include the Narmada, Tapi, and Mahi rivers.

questions.question: From which state to which state do the Eastern Coastal Plains of India extend?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**West Bengal to Tamil Nadu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Eastern Coastal Plains of India extend from **West Bengal in the north to Tamil Nadu in the south**, running along the eastern coastline of India.
 
• They are bordered by the **Bay of Bengal** on the east and the Eastern Ghats on the west.
 
• The plains are divided into two sub-regions: the **Utkal Plains** in Odisha and the **Coromandel Coast** in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
 
• These plains are characterized by several major rivers like the **Ganga, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri**, which form fertile deltas in this region.
 
• The region supports intensive agriculture, particularly of crops like **rice, coconut, and sugarcane**, due to the availability of fertile alluvial soil.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Eastern Coastal Plains:**

 
 
• These are wide, flat plains formed by the depositional activity of rivers.
 
• They are broader and more fertile compared to the Western Coastal Plains of India.
 
 
 
• **Major Deltas:**
 
 
• The region is home to some of the largest deltas in the world, such as the **Sundarbans Delta (Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta)** and the **Godavari-Krishna Delta**.
 
 
 
• **Climate:**
 
 
• The Eastern Coastal Plains experience a tropical monsoon climate with high humidity and significant rainfall, especially during the northeast monsoon season.
 
 
 
• **Ports and Harbors:**
 
 
• Major ports like **Chennai, Visakhapatnam, and Paradip** are located along the Eastern Coastal Plains, playing a significant role in trade and commerce.
 
 
 
• **Biodiversity:**
 
 
• The region includes ecologically significant areas such as the **Sundarbans Mangrove Forests**, which are home to the Royal Bengal Tiger and other endangered species.

questions.question: Which of the following Indian states does NOT have a coastline?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajasthan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Rajasthan** is a landlocked state located in the northwestern part of India and does not have a coastline.
 
• It is bordered by Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat, along with an international border with Pakistan.
 
• States with coastlines in India include Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, and Gujarat, among others, as they are adjacent to the Bay of Bengal or Arabian Sea.
 
• Rajasthan is known for its desert landscape, particularly the Thar Desert, which significantly influences its geography and climate.
 
• As a landlocked state, Rajasthan relies on other states for access to ports and maritime trade.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **India's Coastline:** India has a vast coastline of approximately 7,517 kilometers, with states like Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, and West Bengal having coastal access.
 
• **Landlocked States:** Apart from Rajasthan, other landlocked states in India include Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and others that lack direct access to the sea.
 
• **Thar Desert:** Covering much of Rajasthan, the Thar Desert is the world's 17th largest desert and the 9th largest subtropical desert.
 
• **Importance of Coastlines:** Coastal states significantly contribute to India's economy through trade, fishing, and tourism, as they have access to ports and maritime routes.
 
• **Geographical Diversity:** India showcases diverse geography, including mountains, plains, plateaus, deserts, and coastal regions, which influence the lifestyle and economic activities of its population.

questions.question: The 24° latitude passes closest to which Indian state’s capital?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bhopal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__ 

__
 
• The 24º latitude passes closest to the capital city of **Bhopal**, which is the capital of the Indian state of Madhya Pradesh.
 
• Bhopal is situated at approximately **23.25° N latitude** and **77.41° E longitude**, making it the closest to the 24º N latitude line among the given options.
 
• Other state capitals mentioned in the options, such as Patna, Raipur, and Dispur, are located farther away from the 24º latitude line.
 
• Madhya Pradesh lies in central India, making it geographically closer to the Tropic of Cancer, which is at 23.5º N latitude.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• **Tropic of Cancer:**

 
 
• The Tropic of Cancer is an imaginary line located at 23.5º N latitude, marking the northernmost point where the sun can appear directly overhead during the June solstice.
 
• It passes through eight states in India: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, and Mizoram.
 
 
 
• **Bhopal's Significance:**
 
 
• Bhopal is known as the "City of Lakes" due to its numerous natural and artificial lakes.
 
• It is one of the greenest cities in India and serves as the administrative headquarters of Madhya Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Latitude:**
 
 
• Latitude is a geographic coordinate that specifies the north-south position of a point on the Earth's surface.
 
• Lines of latitude are often referred to as parallels and run horizontally around the globe.
 
 
 
• **Geographical Importance of Madhya Pradesh:**
 
 
• Madhya Pradesh is referred to as the "Heart of India" due to its central location.
 
• The state is rich in cultural heritage and biodiversity, hosting several UNESCO World Heritage Sites and wildlife reserves.

questions.question: Which of the following farming practices is mostly practised in Northeast India and causes soil erosion?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Shifting agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Shifting agriculture**, also known as **Jhum cultivation**, is a traditional farming method practiced in Northeast India, particularly in states like **Assam, Nagaland, and Mizoram**.
 
• Farmers clear forested land by cutting and burning vegetation (**slash-and-burn method**) and use the ash as fertilizer for crops.
 
• This practice leads to severe **soil erosion** due to the removal of vegetation cover, exposing the soil to heavy rainfall and wind.
 
• Shifting agriculture results in the loss of soil nutrients over time, leading to the degradation of land and reduced agricultural productivity.
 
• After a few years, the land is abandoned, and farmers move to another area, repeating the cycle, which further contributes to deforestation and environmental concerns.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Soil Erosion:**

 
 
• It refers to the removal of the topsoil layer due to natural forces like wind and water or human activities such as deforestation and farming.
 
• Soil erosion reduces fertility, destroys agricultural land, and affects water quality in nearby rivers and streams.
 
 
 
• **Terrace Farming:**
 
 
• This is a sustainable agricultural practice where crops are grown on stepped terraces built into hillsides to prevent soil erosion and water runoff.
 
• It is widely practiced in hilly regions, such as in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, but is not the main method used in Northeast India.
 
 
 
• **Mixed Farming:**
 
 
• Involves growing crops and raising livestock simultaneously on the same farm.
 
• It does not involve practices that lead to significant soil erosion.
 
 
 
• **Deforestation:**
 
 
• Shifting agriculture contributes to deforestation as large areas of forests are cleared for farming.
 
• Deforestation leads to loss of biodiversity, disruption of ecosystems, and increased carbon emissions.

questions.question: What is the major constraint in dry land farming?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Low water availability**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Dryland farming **refers to agricultural practices in regions where rainfall is insufficient, typically less than **750 mm annually**, making water availability a critical constraint.
 
• The primary challenge in dryland farming is **low soil moisture** due to minimal rainfall, which limits crop growth and productivity.
 
• Crops grown in such areas are primarily **drought-resistant varieties**, such as millets, sorghum, and pulses, as they can survive with limited water.
 
• Dryland farming areas are also prone to **soil erosion**, which further reduces the land's capacity to retain water.
 
• Efficient water management techniques, such as rainwater harvesting and mulching, are critical to overcoming water scarcity in these regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dryland Farming:**

 
 
• It is a type of farming practiced in arid and semi-arid regions with low rainfall.
 
• Relies on moisture conservation techniques like **deep plowing**, contour farming, and minimal tillage to retain soil moisture.
 
• Crops such as pearl millet, chickpeas, and groundnuts are commonly grown in dryland farming systems.
 
 
 
• **Soil Moisture Management:**
 
 
• Techniques like **mulching** (covering soil with organic matter) help conserve moisture and prevent evaporation.
 
• Use of **micro-irrigation systems**, such as drip irrigation, ensures precise water delivery to crops.
 
 
 
• **Rainwater Harvesting:**
 
 
• Collecting and storing rainwater for agricultural use is a common practice in dryland regions.
 
• Helps supplement water availability during dry spells.
 
 
 
• **Drought-Resistant Crops:**
 
 
• These crops have evolved to survive with minimal water, making them ideal for dryland farming.
 
• Examples include **millets, sorghum, pigeon peas**, and certain oilseeds like sesame.

questions.question: What was the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) in India according to the Sample Registration System (SRS), 2019?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**30 per 1000 live births**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the **Sample Registration System (SRS) 2019**, the **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)** in India was **30 per 1000 live births**.
 
• IMR represents the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per 1000 live births in a given year.
 
• India has witnessed a consistent decline in IMR over the years due to improvements in healthcare, sanitation, and immunization coverage.
 
• The IMR in rural areas was higher at **34 per 1000 live births** compared to urban areas, which recorded **20 per 1000 live births**.
 
• This decline in IMR aligns with the government’s efforts under programs like **National Health Mission (NHM)** and **Intensified Mission Indradhanush**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sample Registration System (SRS):**

 
 
• SRS is a demographic survey conducted in India by the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner**.
 
• It provides reliable annual estimates of birth rates, death rates, and other fertility and mortality indicators.
 
 
 
• **Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR):**
 
 
• NMR refers to the number of deaths of newborns within the first 28 days of life per 1000 live births.
 
• India’s NMR in 2019 stood at **22 per 1000 live births**, as per SRS data.
 
 
 
• **National Health Mission (NHM):**
 
 
• The NHM aims to improve healthcare access and outcomes, particularly for women and children.
 
• It includes initiatives like Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) and Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK).
 
 
 
• **Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI):**
 
 
• IMI aims to achieve full immunization coverage for children under two years and pregnant women.
 
• It targets unvaccinated and partially vaccinated children in underserved areas.
 
 
 
• **Sustainable Development Goals (SDG):**
 
 
• India is committed to reducing IMR and NMR in alignment with SDG 3, which focuses on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all at all ages.

questions.question: Which of the following is a major river of the Indus basin system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ravi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Ravi** is one of the major rivers of the Indus basin system, flowing through India and Pakistan.
 
• The river originates in the **Kullu hills of Himachal Pradesh, India**, and flows westward before entering Pakistan.
 
• It is an important tributary of the Indus River and plays a significant role in the irrigation systems in both countries.
 
• The Ravi River is historically significant, being mentioned in ancient texts like the Rigveda and associated with the region of Punjab.
 
• Under the **Indus Waters Treaty (1960)**, the Ravi is allocated to India for utilization of its waters.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indus River System**

 
 
• The Indus River System consists of six main rivers: Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej.
 
• These rivers originate in the Himalayas and serve as lifelines for agriculture in northern India and Pakistan.
 
• The system is governed by the **Indus Waters Treaty (1960)**, signed between India and Pakistan.
 
 
 
• **Indus Waters Treaty (1960)**
 
 
• The treaty was brokered by the World Bank to resolve water-sharing disputes between India and Pakistan.
 
• Under the treaty, India has control over the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej), while Pakistan controls the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab).
 
 
 
• **Punjab Region**
 
 
• The name "Punjab" translates to "Land of Five Rivers," referring to Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, Chenab, and Jhelum.
 
• The region is agriculturally rich, largely due to the extensive irrigation supported by the Indus River System.
 
 
 
• **Ravi River's Historical Significance**
 
 
• The Ravi River was central to the ancient Indus Valley Civilization.
 
• It flows near the historic city of Lahore, Pakistan, and has cultural importance in the region.

questions.question: Which of the following rivers is NOT a tributary of the Ganga but flows directly into the Bay of Bengal?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahanadi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Mahanadi River** originates from the Sihawa hills in Chhattisgarh and flows through Odisha before emptying directly into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• Unlike rivers such as the Ghaghara, Kosi, and Gomti, which are tributaries of the Ganga, the Mahanadi is an independent river system.
 
• The Mahanadi is one of the major rivers of peninsular India, with a total length of approximately 858 kilometers.
 
• Its basin covers parts of Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, and Madhya Pradesh, making it a significant river for these regions.
 
• Important cities located along the Mahanadi include Sambalpur and Cuttack, with the Hirakud Dam being a notable landmark.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tributaries of the Ganga:**

 
 
• The Ganga River has several tributaries, including the Ghaghara, Kosi, Gomti, Yamuna, Gandak, and Son.
 
• These tributaries contribute significantly to the Ganga's flow and its extensive drainage basin.
 
 
 
• **Rivers flowing into the Bay of Bengal:**
 
 
• Rivers such as the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri flow directly into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• These rivers are part of the peninsular river systems and are not connected to the Ganga.
 
 
 
• **Hirakud Dam on the Mahanadi:**
 
 
• The Hirakud Dam, located near Sambalpur in Odisha, is one of the longest earthen dams in the world.
 
• It plays a crucial role in irrigation, flood control, and hydroelectric power generation.
 
 
 
• **Bay of Bengal:**
 
 
• The Bay of Bengal is the northeastern part of the Indian Ocean and serves as the final destination for several major rivers of India.
 
• It supports diverse ecosystems and acts as a vital economic zone for regional countries.

questions.question: What is the total length of the Mahanadi river?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**851 km**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Mahanadi River has a total length of **851 km**, making it one of the major rivers in central and eastern India.
 
• It originates from **Sihawa in Chhattisgarh** and flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• The river is known for its vast delta and extensive irrigation network, playing a vital role in agriculture and water resources in the region.
 
• It is an important source of water for **Hirakud Dam**, which is one of the largest dams in India and provides irrigation, flood control, and hydroelectric power.
 
• The Mahanadi drainage basin spreads across several states, including Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, and Maharashtra.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hirakud Dam**

 
 
• Located on the Mahanadi River, it is the **longest earthen dam in India**.
 
• It was constructed in 1957 and plays a key role in flood control, irrigation, and hydroelectric power generation.
 
• The reservoir created by the dam spans an area of approximately 743 sq. km.
 
 
 
• **Mahanadi Basin**
 
 
• The Mahanadi Basin covers an area of approximately **141,600 sq. km**.
 
• It includes tributaries such as the Seonath, Mand, Ib, and Hasdeo rivers.
 
• The basin supports agriculture and industries in Chhattisgarh and Odisha.
 
 
 
• **Delta Formation**
 
 
• The Mahanadi forms a wide delta at its mouth near Cuttack in Odisha.
 
• The delta is fertile and heavily cultivated, supporting rice farming and other crops.
 
• It houses several cities and towns, including Paradip Port, which is a key trading hub.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Significance**
 
 
• The Mahanadi River is home to rich biodiversity, including several freshwater fish and aquatic species.
 
• Efforts are being made to address pollution and over-extraction of water from the river.
 
• Conservation initiatives focus on maintaining the ecological balance of the river and its surroundings.

questions.question: In India, irrigation projects with a Cultivable Command Area (CCA) of more than 10,000 hectares are classified as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Major Projects**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Irrigation projects in India are categorized based on their **Cultivable Command Area (CCA)**, which refers to the area that can be irrigated by the project.
 
• Projects with a CCA of more than 10,000 hectares are classified as **Major Projects**.
 
• Major irrigation projects are usually large-scale initiatives involving substantial investment and resources for construction and maintenance.
 
• These projects often include dams, canals, and reservoirs designed to provide water for irrigation, drinking, hydropower generation, and flood control.
 
• Examples of major irrigation projects in India include the Bhakra-Nangal Project, Hirakud Dam, and Nagarjuna Sagar Dam.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cultivable Command Area (CCA):**

 
 
• Refers to the total area that can be irrigated using the water resources available from an irrigation project.
 
• It is a key criterion for classifying irrigation projects in India as Minor, Medium, or Major.
 
 
 
• **Minor Irrigation Projects:**
 
 
• These projects have a CCA of up to 2,000 hectares.
 
• They are typically managed at the local or community level and involve small-scale infrastructure like tanks or wells.
 
 
 
• **Medium Irrigation Projects:**
 
 
• Projects with a CCA between 2,000 and 10,000 hectares fall under this category.
 
• They are more extensive than minor projects but smaller than major ones, involving moderate infrastructure development.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Major Projects in India:**
 
 
• **Bhakra-Nangal Project:** A major multipurpose project on the Sutlej River.
 
• **Nagarjuna Sagar Dam:** One of the largest masonry dams in the world, located on the Krishna River.
 
• **Hirakud Dam:** Built on the Mahanadi River, it is one of the longest earthen dams globally.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Major Irrigation Projects:**
 
 
• They play a crucial role in improving agricultural productivity and ensuring water availability in arid and semi-arid regions.
 
• These projects also support hydropower generation, flood management, and drinking water supply.

questions.question: Which period in India's demographic history is marked by a sharp decline in mortality and persistently high fertility rates?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Phase III (1951–1981)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Phase III (1951–1981) of India's demographic history is characterized by a **sharp decline in mortality rates** due to advancements in healthcare, sanitation, and disease control.
 
• Despite the decline in mortality, fertility rates remained persistently high during this period, leading to significant population growth.
 
• The **Green Revolution** in the 1960s contributed to improved food security, further reducing mortality rates.
 
• This period saw increased efforts in public health programs, including **vaccination drives** and campaigns to reduce communicable diseases such as malaria.
 
• The demographic trends during Phase III led to a phenomenon called the **population explosion** in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mortality Rate:**

 
 
• Mortality rate refers to the number of deaths in a population per unit time, often expressed per 1,000 individuals annually.
 
• Advancements in healthcare during Phase III drastically reduced infant and maternal mortality rates.
 
 
 
• **Fertility Rate:**
 
 
• Fertility rate is the average number of children born to a woman during her lifetime.
 
• High fertility rates during Phase III were influenced by social and cultural norms, low contraceptive usage, and lack of family planning awareness.
 
 
 
• **Population Explosion:**
 
 
• Population explosion refers to rapid population growth due to a significant difference between birth rates and mortality rates.
 
• Phase III witnessed this phenomenon, which posed challenges for resource allocation and economic development.
 
 
 
• **Green Revolution:**
 
 
• The Green Revolution introduced high-yield crop varieties and modern agricultural practices, ensuring food security in India.
 
• It played a crucial role in reducing famine-related mortality rates during Phase III.

questions.question: Which of the following regions in India is known for the Shola forests?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Western Ghats**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Shola forests** are tropical montane forests found in the valleys of the **Western Ghats**, a mountain range running parallel to the western coast of India.
 
• These forests are typically located in the higher altitudes of the Western Ghats, primarily in the states of **Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu**.
 
• The Shola forests are interspersed with grasslands and are known for their rich biodiversity, including several endemic flora and fauna species.
 
• They play a crucial role in maintaining the water cycle in the region by acting as a natural water reservoir and supporting major river systems.
 
• Shola forests are part of the **Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve**, which is a UNESCO-designated area for the conservation of biodiversity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Western Ghats**

 
 
• The Western Ghats, also known as the Sahyadri Hills, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the eight "hottest hotspots" of biological diversity in the world.
 
• They stretch from Gujarat to Kerala, covering a distance of about 1,600 km.
 
• The region is home to a variety of ecosystems, including rainforests, deciduous forests, and montane forests like Sholas.
 
• The Western Ghats significantly influence the monsoon weather pattern in peninsular India.
 
 
 
• **Endemic Flora and Fauna**
 
 
• Shola forests host a variety of endemic species like the Nilgiri Tahr, Lion-tailed Macaque, and the Malabar Civet.
 
• Plant species such as the Nilgiri Rhododendron and Strobilanthes kunthiana (Neelakurinji) are also unique to this region.
 
• The biodiversity of Shola forests is under threat due to deforestation, habitat loss, and climate change.
 
 
 
• **Conservation Efforts**
 
 
• The Western Ghats are protected under various national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, and reserve forests.
 
• Efforts like afforestation, watershed management, and eco-tourism are being promoted to preserve the Shola-grassland ecosystem.
 
• Research and monitoring programs are being conducted to study the impact of human activities and climate change on this fragile ecosystem.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Shola Forests**
 
 
• These forests are critical for water conservation as they feed into several rivers like the Kaveri, Periyar, and Bharathapuzha.
 
• They act as a natural carbon sink, helping mitigate climate change.
 
• The Shola-grassland ecosystem also supports local communities by providing resources like medicinal plants and grazing land.

questions.question: Which state has the longest coastline in mainland India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gujarat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gujarat has the longest coastline among mainland Indian states, measuring approximately **2340 kilometres**.
 
• The coastline of Gujarat is strategically significant as it houses important ports like **Kandla, Mundra, and Pipavav**.
 
• Gujarat's coastline spans the Arabian Sea, facilitating extensive trade and maritime activities.
 
• The state has a rich marine biodiversity and several coastal ecosystems, including mangroves and coral reefs.
 
• Gujarat's coastline plays a crucial role in its economy, contributing significantly to industries such as fisheries, shipbuilding, and salt production.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Coastline in India:**

 
 
• India has a total coastline of **approximately 11,098.81** kilometers, including island territories.
 
• Mainland India's coastline stretches across nine states, with Gujarat having the longest.
 
• Coastal areas are vital for India's economy, supporting ports, trade, fishing, and tourism.
 
 
 
• **Important Ports in Gujarat:**
 
 
• **Kandla Port:** One of India's major ports, known for handling crude oil and petroleum products.
 
• **Mundra Port:** India's largest private port, facilitating significant trade volumes.
 
• **Pipavav Port:** A key port for container and cargo operations.
 
 
 
• **Marine Biodiversity of Gujarat:**
 
 
• The Gulf of Kutch hosts India's first marine national park.
 
• Gujarat's coastline is home to mangroves, coral reefs, and diverse marine species.
 
 
 
• **Economic Importance of Gujarat's Coastline:**
 
 
• Gujarat contributes significantly to India's salt production due to its coastal geography.
 
• The fishing industry along Gujarat's coast supports livelihoods and exports.
 
• Shipbuilding and maritime trade are prominent industries in the region.

questions.question: Which factor plays the most dominant role in the seasonal reversal of wind direction in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Monsoonal pressure system**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The seasonal reversal of wind direction in India is primarily driven by the **monsoonal pressure system**, which is influenced by differential heating of land and water surfaces.
 
• During summer, intense heating of the Indian subcontinent creates a **low-pressure area over northern India**, attracting moisture-laden winds from the Indian Ocean.
 
• In winter, the land cools down rapidly, forming a **high-pressure area**, while the Indian Ocean remains relatively warm, causing winds to reverse direction.
 
• The monsoonal pressure system is a key feature of India's climate and is responsible for **seasonal rainfall patterns**, which are crucial for agriculture and water resources.
 
• This dynamic system is heavily influenced by the **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)**, which shifts northward during summer and southward during winter.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Monsoon Definition:** The term "monsoon" originates from the Arabic word "mausim," meaning season. It refers to the seasonal wind patterns driven by temperature and pressure differences between land and sea.
 
• **Southwest Monsoon:** Occurs during summer (June–September) when winds blow from the Indian Ocean towards the Indian subcontinent, bringing heavy rainfall.
 
• **Northeast Monsoon:** Occurs during winter (October–December) when winds reverse direction, carrying dry air from land to sea and resulting in limited rainfall in certain regions.
 
• **Role of ITCZ:** The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone is a belt of low pressure near the equator where trade winds converge. Its north-south movement significantly impacts monsoon dynamics.
 
• **El Niño and La Niña:** These oceanic phenomena can influence monsoon intensity and rainfall patterns by affecting sea surface temperatures and atmospheric circulation.

questions.question: The India-Bhutan boundary is primarily defined by which of these?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mountains and treaties**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The India-Bhutan boundary is primarily defined by the **Himalayan mountain ranges**, which act as a natural border between the two nations.
 
• Several treaties, including the **1949 Treaty of Friendship** and its updated version in 2007, govern the bilateral relationship and border agreements between India and Bhutan.
 
• Bhutan shares a border of approximately **699 km** with Indian states such as Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, West Bengal, and Sikkim.
 
• India and Bhutan have maintained **peaceful relations** along the border, largely attributed to mutual cooperation and historical treaties.
 
• No significant fencing exists along the India-Bhutan border, as both countries rely on natural geographical features and diplomatic agreements for border management.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Himalayan Mountain Ranges**

 
 
• The Himalayas act as a natural barrier between India and its northern neighbors, including Bhutan, Nepal, and China.
 
• They are characterized by **high-altitude terrains**, dense forests, and glacial rivers.
 
• The Himalayan ranges influence the climatic patterns and ecosystems of the region.
 
 
 
• **1949 Treaty of Friendship**
 
 
• This treaty established India and Bhutan as close allies, ensuring **mutual respect and cooperation**.
 
• It included provisions for **non-interference in each other's internal affairs**, while India supported Bhutan in its foreign relations.
 
 
 
• **2007 Treaty Update**
 
 
• The treaty was revised to provide **greater autonomy** to Bhutan in its foreign policy decisions.
 
• It reinforced the peaceful and cooperative nature of the India-Bhutan relationship.
 
 
 
• **Geopolitical Importance of Bhutan**
 
 
• Bhutan serves as a **buffer state** between India and China, contributing to regional stability.
 
• The strategic location of Bhutan makes it crucial for India's **security and foreign policy**.

questions.question: What type of coastal plain are the Western Coastal Plains of India classified as?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Submerged Coastal Plain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Western Coastal Plains of India are classified as **submerged coastal plains**, formed due to the submergence of landmass along the western coastline.
 
• This type of plain features narrow coastal strips with lagoons, estuaries, and backwaters commonly found in regions like Kerala.
 
• The submergence of land has resulted in characteristic landforms such as **rivers flowing into the Arabian Sea forming estuaries**, unlike the deltas formed in the eastern coastal plains.
 
• Prominent features of the Western Coastal Plains include **the Konkan Coast (Maharashtra), the Malabar Coast (Kerala), and the Kannad Coast (Karnataka)**.
 
• The submerged nature of the plains makes them rich in aquatic biodiversity, supporting fisheries and other marine activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Submerged Coastal Plain:**

 
 
• These plains are formed when coastal regions sink below sea level due to tectonic movements or rising sea levels.
 
• Submerged plains often feature estuaries, lagoons, and submerged valleys.
 
• Examples include the Western Coastal Plains of India and parts of the eastern United States coastline.
 
 
 
• **Eastern Coastal Plains vs Western Coastal Plains:**
 
 
• Eastern Coastal Plains are emergent plains, characterized by wide deltas of rivers like the Ganga, Godavari, and Krishna.
 
• Western Coastal Plains are submerged plains, with narrow coastal strips and estuaries formed by rivers flowing into the Arabian Sea.
 
 
 
• **Estuaries:**
 
 
• An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal body of water where freshwater from rivers meets and mixes with saltwater from the sea.
 
• Estuaries are rich in biodiversity and serve as critical habitats for various aquatic species.
 
 
 
• **Backwaters:**
 
 
• Backwaters are brackish lagoons or lakes lying parallel to the coast, formed due to the action of waves and tides.
 
• Kerala is famous for its extensive network of backwaters, such as Vembanad Lake.

questions.question: Which of the following soils has the highest water-retaining capacity?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Black Soil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Black soil**, also known as Regur soil, has the highest water-retaining capacity due to its high clay content.
 
• It is predominantly found in the **Deccan Plateau regions** of India, including Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu.
 
• The soil is rich in nutrients like calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash, and lime, which further enhance its ability to retain moisture.
 
• Black soil is highly suitable for cultivating crops like **cotton, sugarcane, wheat, and pulses** due to its moisture-retaining ability.
 
• Its unique property of forming deep cracks during dry seasons helps in air circulation and improves soil fertility.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Water-retaining capacity:**

 
 
• This refers to the ability of soil to hold water and make it available for plant growth.
 
• Clayey soils, like black soil, have a higher water-retaining capacity compared to sandy soils.
 
 
 
• **Red Soil:**
 
 
• Found in areas with high iron oxide content, giving it a reddish appearance.
 
• It has low water-retaining capacity and is less fertile compared to black soil.
 
 
 
• **Alluvial Soil:**
 
 
• Highly fertile and found in river basins, but its water-retaining capacity is moderate.
 
• Suitable for crops like rice, wheat, and sugarcane.
 
 
 
• **Desert Soil:**
 
 
• Found in arid regions like Rajasthan and Gujarat.
 
• It is sandy, has very low water-retaining capacity, and requires irrigation for cultivation.
 
 
 
• **Clay content importance:**
 
 
• Clay particles are small and have a high surface area, allowing them to retain moisture effectively.
 
• Soils with higher clay content are generally better at holding water and nutrients.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of subsistence farming?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Use of high-end machinery**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Subsistence farming** is characterized by small-scale farming aimed at meeting the basic needs of the farmer's family rather than producing surplus for trade.
 
• It typically relies on **family labour**, where members of the household work together to cultivate crops and rear livestock.
 
• Manual agricultural practices such as the use of simple tools and traditional methods are prevalent in subsistence farming.
 
• Farmers often use **traditional seed varieties** that are locally adapted and passed down through generations.
 
• The use of high-end machinery is not a feature of subsistence farming, as it is often financially inaccessible and unnecessary for small-scale operations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Subsistence Farming:**

 
 
• It is practiced primarily in developing countries, where farmers grow food mainly for their own consumption.
 
• Subsistence farming is often rain-fed and depends heavily on natural soil fertility.
 
• Crops grown include staple foods such as rice, wheat, maize, and root crops like cassava.
 
 
 
• **Commercial Farming:**
 
 
• In contrast to subsistence farming, commercial farming involves large-scale production for trade and profit.
 
• High-end machinery, advanced irrigation systems, and genetically modified seeds are commonly used in commercial farming.
 
• It is heavily reliant on market demand and economic factors.
 
 
 
• **Traditional Seed Varieties:**
 
 
• These are seeds that have been cultivated, saved, and passed down through generations by farmers.
 
• They are often more resistant to local pests and diseases compared to hybrid or genetically modified seeds.
 
• Traditional seeds are essential for preserving biodiversity and promoting sustainable agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Mechanization in Agriculture:**
 
 
• Mechanization refers to the use of advanced machinery and technology to enhance agricultural productivity.
 
• It is typically more prominent in large-scale commercial farming.
 
• Examples include tractors, harvesters, and irrigation systems.

questions.question: In India, which of the following is a groundwater-based irrigation source?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Open-well**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Open-wells are one of the most common sources of **groundwater-based irrigation** in India, particularly in rural areas.
 
• These wells are manually or mechanically dug to access groundwater, which is then used for irrigation purposes.
 
• Open-wells do not require advanced drilling technology, making them cost-effective and accessible for small and marginal farmers.
 
• This irrigation method relies on natural recharge processes, such as rainfall, to replenish the groundwater.
 
• Open-wells are widely used in regions where groundwater is available at shallow depths, such as parts of peninsular India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Groundwater Irrigation in India:**

 
 
• Groundwater irrigation accounts for nearly **63% of the total irrigated area** in India, making it the largest source of irrigation.
 
• It is primarily extracted using open-wells, tube wells, and bore wells.
 
• States like Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Bihar are major users of groundwater for irrigation.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Surface Water Irrigation:**
 
 
• Surface water irrigation uses sources like rivers, canals, ponds, and tanks, while groundwater irrigation depends on aquifers and underground reserves.
 
• Groundwater irrigation is independent of surface water flow, making it more reliable during dry seasons.
 
 
 
• **Challenges of Groundwater Irrigation:**
 
 
• Over-extraction of groundwater can lead to depletion of aquifers and falling water tables.
 
• Regions like Punjab and Haryana are facing critical groundwater stress due to excessive irrigation for water-intensive crops like paddy.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives for Sustainable Irrigation:**
 
 
• Programs like **Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY)** aim to promote efficient water use and reduce dependence on groundwater.
 
• Micro-irrigation techniques like drip and sprinkler irrigation are being encouraged to save water and ensure sustainable farming.

questions.question: In India, a city with a population of less than 10,000 and more than 5000 is classified as which type of class town?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Class V**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In India, cities are classified into different classes based on their population size as per the Census of India.
 
• A city with a population of **5,000 to 9,999** falls under the classification of **Class V town**.
 
• The classification helps in urban planning and allocation of resources for development based on population density.
 
• Class I towns have populations exceeding 100,000, while Class VI towns have populations less than 5,000.
 
• The Census of India defines six population classes, ranging from Class I to Class VI, for better administrative and demographic categorization.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Population Classification in India:**

 
 
• Class I: Population exceeding 100,000.
 
• Class II: Population between 50,000 to 99,999.
 
• Class III: Population between 20,000 to 49,999.
 
• Class IV: Population between 10,000 to 19,999.
 
• Class V: Population between 5,000 to 9,999.
 
• Class VI: Population less than 5,000.
 
 
 
• **Purpose of Classification:** It assists in urban development planning, policymaking, and resource allocation.
 
• **Census of India:** Conducted every 10 years, the Census provides crucial demographic data on population distribution, literacy, sex ratio, and urbanization.
 
• **Urbanization Trends:** India is witnessing rapid urbanization, with a significant increase in the number of Class I towns over the decades.
 
• **Historical Context:** Population classification was introduced during British rule for administrative purposes and has continued post-independence to guide development efforts.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a surrounding feature of the Thar Desert?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vindhya Hills**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Thar Desert, also known as the Great Indian Desert, is primarily located in the northwestern part of India and southeastern Pakistan.
 
• Surrounding features of the Thar Desert include the Aravalli Range, Rann of Kachchh, and the Indus River Plain.
 
• The Vindhya Hills are geographically situated farther south and do not form part of the surrounding features of the Thar Desert.
 
• The Thar Desert is bordered by the Rann of Kachchh in Gujarat to the southwest and the Aravalli Range to the southeast.
 
• The Indus River Plain lies to the west of the Thar Desert and forms part of its broader geographical context.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Thar Desert Geography:**

 
 
• The Thar Desert spans approximately 200,000 square kilometers and covers parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab, and Haryana in India.
 
• It is characterized by sandy terrain, dunes, sparse vegetation, and extreme temperature variations.
 
 
 
• **Aravalli Range:**
 
 
• The Aravalli Range is one of the oldest mountain ranges in India and acts as a natural barrier between the Thar Desert and the fertile regions of eastern Rajasthan.
 
• It plays a significant role in influencing the climate and ecology of the Thar Desert.
 
 
 
• **Rann of Kachchh:**
 
 
• Located in Gujarat, the Rann of Kachchh is a salt marsh and forms the southwestern boundary of the Thar Desert.
 
• It is known for its unique ecosystem and the famous Rann Utsav cultural festival.
 
 
 
• **Vindhya Hills:**
 
 
• The Vindhya Hills are located in central India and are considered a geographical divide between northern and southern India.
 
• They do not have a direct connection to the Thar Desert's geographical features.
 
 
 
• **Indus River Plain:**
 
 
• The Indus River Plain lies to the west of the Thar Desert and is part of the broader drainage system of the region.
 
• This plain is fertile and contrasts with the arid conditions of the Thar Desert.

questions.question: What is the significance of Westerly Jet Streams in winter?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Guide Western Disturbances into India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Westerly Jet Streams** are fast-moving air currents in the upper atmosphere that significantly influence weather patterns during winter.
 
• These jet streams play a key role in guiding **Western Disturbances**, which are extratropical storms originating in the Mediterranean region, into the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Western Disturbances bring **rainfall and snowfall** to northern and northwestern India during winter, particularly in the states of Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand.
 
• The Westerly Jet Streams are strongest during winter months due to the temperature gradient between the tropics and polar regions.
 
• These jet streams significantly influence **agricultural activities** in India, as the precipitation from Western Disturbances supports Rabi crops like wheat and barley.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Western Disturbances:**

 
 
• Western Disturbances are weather systems characterized by low-pressure areas and are carried into India by Westerly Jet Streams.
 
• They originate over the Mediterranean Sea, Caspian Sea, and Black Sea regions.
 
• These disturbances cause **rainfall and snowfall** in the Himalayan region during winter months.
 
• They are crucial for maintaining the winter crop cycle in northern India.
 
 
 
• **Jet Streams:**
 
 
• Jet streams are narrow bands of strong winds in the upper levels of the atmosphere.
 
• They are typically found at altitudes of 9-12 km above the Earth's surface.
 
• Jet streams are caused by the temperature contrast between tropical and polar regions.
 
• The two major jet streams influencing India are the Westerly Jet Stream (winter) and the Easterly Jet Stream (summer).
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Climate:**
 
 
• In winter, Westerly Jet Streams guide Western Disturbances, causing rainfall over northwestern India and the Himalayas.
 
• In summer, the Easterly Jet Streams contribute to the onset of the Indian monsoon.
 
• Jet streams significantly affect the distribution and intensity of rainfall in India.
 
• They also influence temperature patterns and seasonal shifts in weather systems.
 
 
 
• **Rabi Crops:**
 
 
• Rabi crops are winter crops sown in October-November and harvested in March-April.
 
• Wheat, barley, mustard, and peas are examples of Rabi crops.
 
• Rainfall from Western Disturbances during winter is essential for their cultivation.
 
• Regions dependent on Rabi crops are particularly affected by variations in Westerly Jet Streams.

questions.question: Which of the following is the largest contributor to irrigation in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tube wells and canals**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tube wells and canals account for the largest share of irrigation in India**, contributing significantly to agricultural productivity.
 
• Canals are prominent irrigation sources in areas like Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh due to their extensive network and water availability.
 
• **Tube wells** rely on groundwater extraction, making them widely used in regions with low surface water availability, such as Rajasthan and parts of Maharashtra.
 
• The **Green Revolution** further promoted the use of tube wells and canals, especially in northern India, to ensure reliable water supply for high-yield crops.
 
• Together, tube wells and canals irrigate a significant portion of India's agricultural land, ensuring food security for the growing population.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Canal Irrigation:**

 
 
• Canals are artificial waterways that distribute water from rivers or reservoirs to agricultural fields.
 
• They are particularly effective in regions with flat terrain and abundant surface water sources.
 
• India has an extensive canal network, with major projects like the Indira Gandhi Canal in Rajasthan.
 
 
 
• **Tube Wells:**
 
 
• Tube wells are deep bore wells equipped with pumps to extract groundwater for irrigation.
 
• They are widely used in areas where surface water sources are scarce or unreliable.
 
• Excessive use of tube wells has led to groundwater depletion in certain regions, necessitating sustainable practices.
 
 
 
• **Rainwater Harvesting:**
 
 
• Rainwater harvesting involves collecting and storing rainwater for irrigation and other purposes.
 
• Though beneficial, it is a secondary source of irrigation compared to tube wells and canals in India.
 
 
 
• **Tank Irrigation:**
 
 
• Tanks are small water reservoirs used primarily in southern states like Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.
 
• They provide water for irrigation during dry seasons but have limited coverage compared to tube wells and canals.

questions.question: The Eastern Coastal Plains of India are best described as which type of coast?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Emergent coast**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Eastern Coastal Plains of India are classified as an **emergent coast**, which means they have been formed due to the gradual upliftment of land or a fall in sea level.
 
• These plains stretch along the eastern edge of India, covering states like Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and parts of West Bengal.
 
• The region is marked by extensive deltas formed by rivers like the **Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri**, which contribute to the fertile soil.
 
• Emergent coasts are characterized by features such as wide plains, lagoons, backwaters, and riverine estuaries, which are prominent along India’s Eastern Coastal Plains.
 
• These plains are generally flat and low-lying, making them suitable for agriculture and settlement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Emergent Coast:**

 
 
• An emergent coast forms due to tectonic uplift or a drop in sea level, exposing previously submerged areas.
 
• Such coasts often feature raised beaches, marine terraces, and expansive plains.
 
• India’s Eastern Coastal Plains are an example, showcasing deltaic formations and fertile lands.
 
 
 
• **Submerged Coast:**
 
 
• Formed due to rising sea levels or subsidence of land, resulting in features such as bays, fjords, and estuaries.
 
• India’s Western Coastal Plains exhibit characteristics of a partially submerged coast.
 
 
 
• **River Deltas:**
 
 
• Rivers like the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri contribute to the formation of fertile deltas along the Eastern Coastal Plains.
 
• These deltas are vital for agriculture and host biodiversity-rich ecosystems.
 
 
 
• **Coastal Importance in India:**
 
 
• The Eastern Coastal Plains are crucial for agriculture, fishing, and port-based trade.
 
• Prominent cities like Chennai, Visakhapatnam, and Kolkata are located along this coast.

questions.question: Which region of the Northern Plains is made of older alluvium?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bhangar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bhangar** is the older alluvium found in the Northern Plains of India.
 
• It is characterized by its slightly elevated terraces compared to the newer alluvium, known as Khadar.
 
• The soil in the Bhangar region is generally **less fertile** due to the presence of lime nodules, locally called **kankar**.
 
• This region is usually found farther away from river courses and is more stable as compared to the younger Khadar regions.
 
• Bhangar plays a crucial role in agriculture but often requires more effort to improve soil fertility compared to Khadar.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Khadar:** The newer alluvium deposited by rivers during floods, forming fertile plains ideal for agriculture.
 
• **Bhabar:** A narrow belt of coarse gravel and pebbles situated at the foothills of the Himalayas, where rivers disappear due to high porosity.
 
• **Terai:** A marshy region located south of the Bhabar belt, where rivers re-emerge, supporting dense vegetation and rich biodiversity.
 
• **Alluvium:** Sediments deposited by rivers, categorized into older (Bhangar) and newer (Khadar) based on their time of deposition and fertility.
 
• The Northern Plains of India are formed by the deposition of sediments brought by the **Ganga, Brahmaputra, and Indus river systems.**

questions.question: What type of farming is practised in hill regions by cutting slopes into steps?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Terrace farming**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Terrace farming** is an agricultural method where sloped lands are cut into a series of steps or terraces to create flat surfaces for cultivation.
 
• This method is widely practised in hilly or mountainous regions to prevent soil erosion and water runoff.
 
• It allows farmers to maximize arable land in regions with steep gradients and helps in water conservation by reducing surface runoff.
 
• Terrace farming is commonly found in areas like the Himalayan region, Southeast Asia, and the Andes.
 
• It is particularly suited for crops such as rice, wheat, and maize, which require level surfaces and controlled water flow.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Soil Erosion Prevention:** Terrace farming reduces the speed of water flow on slopes, minimizing soil erosion and preserving fertile topsoil.
 
• **Water Management:** The terraces act as water catchment areas, enabling better water retention and distribution for crops.
 
• **Challenges:** The construction and maintenance of terraces can be labor-intensive and expensive.
 
• **Regions Practicing Terrace Farming:** Notable examples include the rice terraces of the Philippines (e.g., Banaue Rice Terraces) and the Andes Mountains in South America.
 
• **Climate Adaptation:** This technique is also a sustainable farming method that supports agriculture in challenging terrains and climates.

questions.question: In India, which region is NOT suitable for tube-well irrigation due to non-alluvial tracts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Plateau regions**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Plateau regions** in India, such as the **Deccan Plateau**, are characterized by hard rock formations and non-alluvial soil, making them unsuitable for tube-well irrigation.
 
• Tube-well irrigation requires **soft, porous, and permeable alluvial soil** to facilitate water extraction, which is not present in plateau regions.
 
• These regions often lack sufficient groundwater recharge due to rocky terrain and limited aquifer systems.
 
• In contrast, regions like Punjab, Western Uttar Pradesh, and Coastal Plains have fertile alluvial soil and abundant groundwater, making them ideal for tube-well irrigation.
 
• Farmers in plateau regions primarily depend on rainfall or surface water sources such as tanks, reservoirs, and rivers for irrigation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Alluvial Soil and Irrigation:**

 
 
• Alluvial soil is formed by river deposits and is rich in nutrients, making it fertile and ideal for agriculture.
 
• Its porous structure allows easy water percolation, which facilitates the use of tube-well irrigation.
 
 
 
• **Groundwater and Aquifers:**
 
 
• Groundwater is stored in aquifers, which are layers of permeable rock or sediment that can hold and transmit water.
 
• Plateau regions typically have fractured or impermeable rocks that hinder groundwater storage and extraction.
 
 
 
• **Deccan Plateau Characteristics:**
 
 
• It is composed of igneous and metamorphic rocks, which are hard and non-porous.
 
• These features limit the region’s ability to support groundwater-based irrigation systems like tube-wells.
 
 
 
• **Alternative Irrigation in Plateau Regions:**
 
 
• Farmers rely on surface irrigation methods such as canals, tanks, and rainwater harvesting to meet their agricultural water needs.
 
• Government initiatives promote micro-irrigation techniques like drip and sprinkler systems to optimize water use in these areas.
 
 
 
• **Indian Irrigation Practices:**
 
 
• Approximately 48% of India’s net sown area relies on irrigation, with tube-wells being a major source in alluvial regions.
 
• Regions unsuitable for tube-well irrigation often implement watershed development projects to improve water availability.

questions.question: Which country lies to the east of Arunachal Pradesh?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Myanmar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Arunachal Pradesh is located in the northeastern region of India, sharing its eastern border with **Myanmar**.
 
• The border between Arunachal Pradesh and Myanmar is demarcated by the **India-Myanmar International Boundary**.
 
• The border region is characterized by dense forests and mountainous terrain, making it strategically and geographically significant.
 
• Arunachal Pradesh also shares international borders with **China** to the north and Bhutan to the west, but Myanmar lies directly to its east.
 
• This area includes tribal communities and is part of the larger Indo-Burma biodiversity hotspot.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bordering States and Countries:**

 
 
• Arunachal Pradesh shares its borders with three countries: **China, Bhutan, and Myanmar**.
 
• It also shares state borders with Assam and Nagaland within India.
 
 
 
• **McMahon Line:**
 
 
• The McMahon Line is the de facto boundary between India and China in Arunachal Pradesh.
 
• This line is a source of territorial disputes between India and China.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Diversity:**
 
 
• Arunachal Pradesh is home to numerous indigenous tribes, including the Adi, Nyishi, Apatani, and Mishmi tribes.
 
• These tribes have unique cultures, traditions, and languages.
 
 
 
• **Strategic Importance:**
 
 
• Arunachal Pradesh holds strategic importance for India due to its location at the tri-junction of India, China, and Myanmar.
 
• It is critical for India’s border security and regional connectivity initiatives.

questions.question: How many total islands/islets/rocky outcrops are there in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands as per the Andaman and Nicobar Administration?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**836**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The** Andaman and Nicobar Islands** are a group of islands located in the Bay of Bengal, consisting of a total of **836 islands/islets/rocky outcrops** as per the Andaman and Nicobar Administration.
 
• The archipelago is divided into two groups: the Andaman Islands (north) and the Nicobar Islands (south).
 
• These islands are known for their rich biodiversity, unique flora and fauna, and strategic importance for India's maritime boundaries.
 
• Of the 836 islands, only a fraction are inhabited, while the majority remain pristine and untouched.
 
• These islands form a vital ecological hotspot and are protected under various environmental laws and conservation programs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Geographical Significance**

 
 
• The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie at the juncture of the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea, making them strategically important for India's defense and trade.
 
• They act as a natural barrier to the Indian coastline, protecting it from potential threats and offering a vantage point for maritime surveillance.
 
 
 
• **Biodiversity**
 
 
• The islands are part of the Indo-Malayan eco-zone, hosting a variety of endemic species, including rare birds, reptiles, and marine life.
 
• The tropical rainforests here support diverse ecosystems, with mangroves playing a key role in stabilizing coastal environments.
 
 
 
• **Tribes of the Islands**
 
 
• The islands are home to indigenous tribes such as the Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarwa, and Sentinelese.
 
• These tribes have distinct cultural practices and lifestyles, and efforts are made to preserve their heritage and isolation.
 
 
 
• **Tourism and Conservation**
 
 
• The islands are a popular tourist destination, known for their beaches, coral reefs, and adventure activities like scuba diving.
 
• Significant areas are designated as protected zones, such as the Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park, to conserve the delicate ecosystems.
